Issued at 349 PM CDT Wed Sep 16 2026

Scattered showers & thunderstorms develop across western 
Minnesota this evening & spread eastwards through the overnight 
hours as a weak shortwave moves across the region coupled with
an increasing nocturnal low-level jet. Rainfall amounts should 
generally stay light, with most locations receiving around 
0.1-0.25 before showers move east Thursday morning. Some low 
clouds & patchy fog could linger into Thursday morning, but 
otherwise a quiet & seasonably warm day is expected with highs 
in the low to mid 70s. Our attention then quickly turns to a 
much stronger system moving out of the central Plains Thursday 
night into Friday.

Friday through early Saturday continues to be the main weather 
concern over the next seven days. A strengthening low- level jet
will transport an impressive amount of moisture northwards with
PWAT values approaching 2". These values are near the top of 
climatology for mid-September, priming the atmosphere for 
showers & thunderstorms capable of very efficient rainfall 
rates. Atypical of these summer-like precipitable water values 
is the strong upper level forcing, as a shortwave passing 
directly over the region generates strong low & mid- level 
frontogenesis north of a quasi-stationary surface boundary 
across southern Minnesota & Wisconsin. Numerous showers & 
thunderstorms are expected to fire along & north of this 
boundary through the day Friday into early saturday morning, 
with heavy rain & potential flooding where multiple rounds of 
thunderstorms set up over the same areas.

This forcing will begin to peak Friday morning, when the first 
round of heavy rain looks to spread into southern & central 
Minnesota. The heaviest rain looks to fall across southern
Minnesota, but available high-resolution guidances highlights
the potential for a secondary band of frontogenically-forced
rainfall falling farther north across central Minnesota
& Wisconsin. We will also have to monitor the storms across
southern Minnesota for potential severe weather Friday morning
as high- resolution guidance is depicting a gravity-wave induced
damaging wind signature with the thunderstorms. There may be 
somewhat of a break or decrease in coverage during the afternoon
before another, likely heavier round develops Friday evening & 
persists overnight into early Saturday morning. This second 
round is when the best overlap of moisture transport, elevated 
instability, & frontogenetic forcing should occur, making it the
period of greatest concern for training thunderstorms & high 
rainfall rates. Severe weather currently looks like a secondary 
concern given limited surface-based instability, although 
embedded thunderstorms will enhance rainfall rates.

Where exactly the heaviest rain sets up remains the biggest
forecast question. Guidance continues to span solutions from 
central Minnesota southwards to the Iowa border, with the 
broader suite of legacy deterministic models generally a little
farther north, while deterministic & AI ensemble guidance 
continues to favor a more southern axis. For now, we favor this 
farther-south camp, placing the greatest risk for amounts in 
excess of 3-4" from roughly the far-southern Twin Cities metro 
southwards towards the Minnesota/Iowa border, then east through 
southeast Minnesota into western Wisconsin. Localized amounts of
6-8" are certainly possible within this heaviest band of 
rainfall, with much of this rainfall potentially falling in a 
short amount of time overnight Friday into saturday. Amounts are
expected to fall-off rather sharply north of this swath of the 
heaviest rain, although amounts around 1-2" are still likely 
into central Minnesota & west-central Wisconsin. Unfortunately 
for our most- drought stricken areas, little in the rainfall is 
expected across north-central Minnesota & northwest Wisconsin.

Flooding will become a concern wherever the swath of heaviest
rain occurs. Repeated rounds of thunderstorms could produce 
flash flooding in urban & poor- drainage areas along with rises 
on smaller rivers & streams, especially Friday night into early 
Saturday morning when the heaviest rain currently appears most 
likely. Some factors that may help mitigate the flooding threat
(despite the heavy rain amounts) are that antecedent conditions
are still quite dry, & the lull between the expected two round
of heavy rain may help prevent maximum runoff of the rainfall.
Still - now is the time time to have a flood plan in place if
you live in a low-lying or water-senstive area where the
heaviest rain is expected to occur. 

Rain should end from west to east Saturday morning as the 
system pulls away, with much of Saturday afternoon looking drier
& cooler. Another upper low approaches Sunday into early next 
week, bringing additional chances for showers Sunday through 
Monday. These later rounds dont look nearly as heavy at this
